chunks.doc_title: Comparing AI Policy Approaches Across the UAE and Saudi Arabia
chunks.text:
Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia treat artificial intelligence as a pillar of
post-oil economic diversification rather than as a narrow technology
portfolio. The UAE frames this through its National Strategy for Artificial
Intelligence 2031 and the wider Centennial 2071 vision; Saudi Arabia frames it
through the National Strategy for Data and AI under the umbrella of Vision
2030. Both countries set explicit, numeric economic targets rather than only
qualitative ambitions, and both created a dedicated ministerial or
authority-level role years before most peer governments did: the UAE
appointed the world's first Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence in
2017, while Saudi Arabia established SDAIA by royal decree in 2019.

chunks.doc_title: Comparing AI Policy Approaches Across the UAE and Saudi Arabia
chunks.text:
The two countries differ in how they distribute authority. The UAE spreads
responsibility across multiple bodies: the Minister of State for AI sets
policy direction, the Emirates Council for AI and Digital Transactions
coordinates federal and emirate-level execution, the UAE Data Office governs
personal data specifically, and the Cyber Security Council owns AI-specific
security policy. Saudi Arabia concentrates more authority inside a single
authority, SDAIA, which runs both data governance and AI development through
its NDMO and NCAI subsidiaries respectively. Neither structure is obviously
superior; the UAE's distributed model can move on parallel tracks but
requires more coordination, while Saudi Arabia's concentrated model
simplifies accountability but places more load on one institution.

chunks.doc_title: Comparing AI Policy Approaches Across the UAE and Saudi Arabia
chunks.text:
Saudi Arabia has more explicitly separated research from commercialisation,
with SDAIA and NCAI retaining research authority while HUMAIN, backed by the
Public Investment Fund, serves as the commercial and production arm for
advanced models such as ALLaM. The UAE's approach blends sovereign capital
and commercial development more directly through Mubadala and ADQ, which
both fund infrastructure and take direct stakes in AI companies, rather than
channelling that role through a single dedicated commercial entity.

chunks.doc_title: Comparing AI Policy Approaches Across the UAE and Saudi Arabia
chunks.section: Data protection as a shared foundation
chunks.text:
Both countries have moved to establish comprehensive personal data protection
laws as a foundation for trustworthy AI deployment: the UAE's Federal
Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 and Saudi Arabia's Personal Data Protection Law,
developed with SDAIA's involvement. Both laws draw on GDPR as a reference
point while adapting provisions to local legal and administrative structures,
and both explicitly anticipate that AI-driven automated decision-making
creates privacy and oversight obligations beyond ordinary data processing.

chunks.doc_title: Comparing AI Policy Approaches Across the UAE and Saudi Arabia
chunks.section: What this means for AI deployment in the region
chunks.text:
For an organisation or researcher operating across both markets, the
practical implication is that compliance cannot be treated as a single
regional standard: data residency rules, AI security expectations, and
risk-classification frameworks differ enough between the UAE and Saudi Arabia
that GDPR-style compliance, or compliance with one country's framework, does
not transfer automatically to the other. Both jurisdictions are also still in
active rule-making, with Saudi Arabia's AI risk framework still in draft form
and the UAE's AI Security Policy only issued in 2025, so organisations should
expect continued change rather than a settled baseline.

chunks.doc_title: AI Deployment in Gulf Healthcare Systems
chunks.section: Why healthcare is a priority sector
chunks.text:
Both the UAE National AI Strategy 2031 and Saudi Arabia's NSDAI name
healthcare as a priority deployment sector, but for related rather than
identical reasons. The UAE strategy lists healthcare improvement explicitly
among the societal challenges it wants AI to address, alongside traffic
safety, partly through national AI challenges that invite targeted solutions.
Saudi Arabia's interest is shaped heavily by demographic pressure: the
Kingdom's population is growing at roughly 2.43 percent annually, life
expectancy has risen from 66 to 74 years over three decades, and the share of
the population aged 60 or older is projected to reach around 25 percent by
2050, all of which strain a healthcare system already running close to 2.25
hospital beds per 1,000 people across more than 480 hospitals.

chunks.doc_title: AI Deployment in Gulf Healthcare Systems
chunks.text:
SDAIA's National Center for Artificial Intelligence engages directly with
healthcare stakeholders to develop AI use cases in partnership with health
sector bodies, and to support AI research and publications aimed at
generating measurable impact. The strategic premise is that future healthcare
gains will depend not only on traditional clinical data but increasingly on
behavioural, lifestyle, and genomic data, which has pushed Saudi Arabia
toward parallel investment in biotechnology and bioinformatics infrastructure
alongside its core AI strategy.

chunks.doc_title: AI Deployment in Gulf Healthcare Systems
chunks.section: Data governance implications for clinical AI
chunks.text:
Health data occupies a special position in both countries' data protection
regimes. The UAE's Personal Data Protection Law explicitly excludes health
data processed under sector-specific legislation from its general scope,
meaning clinical AI systems are governed by separate health-data rules rather
than the general PDPL. This matters for anyone building clinical machine
learning systems in the region: general-purpose PDPL compliance work does not
automatically cover a healthcare deployment, and a separate assessment
against sector-specific health data rules is typically required.

chunks.doc_title: AI Deployment in Gulf Healthcare Systems
chunks.text:
Saudi Arabia's draft National AI Risk Management Framework introduces a
risk-based classification distinguishing low-risk from high-risk AI systems.
Clinical decision-support tools, diagnostic models, and any AI system whose
output materially affects a patient's treatment would be expected to fall
into the higher-risk tier under this kind of framework, which typically
carries stricter compliance, documentation, and human-oversight requirements
than lower-risk applications such as administrative automation.

chunks.doc_title: AI Deployment in Gulf Healthcare Systems
chunks.section: Practical takeaway for applied ML work
chunks.text:
Building healthcare-relevant AI systems for deployment in the Gulf region
involves at least three distinct compliance surfaces: general data protection
law, sector-specific health data rules, and an emerging risk-classification
layer that is likely to treat clinical applications as high-risk by default.
Researchers and engineers working on clinical datasets, including
de-identified research datasets such as MIMIC-III, should treat regional
deployment compliance as a separate problem from research-stage model
development, since the rules governing a published research model and a
deployed clinical tool in this region are not the same.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.text:
The Saudi Data and Artificial Intelligence Authority, established by royal
decree in 2019, is the Kingdom's central body for both data governance and AI
strategy. SDAIA operates through two principal subsidiaries: the National
Data Management Office, which handles data governance and regulation, and the
National Center for Artificial Intelligence, which leads AI research,
development, and adoption. A third unit, the National Information Center,
supports the broader mandate. This dual structure lets SDAIA pursue
regulatory and promotional goals at the same time, rather than splitting them
across separate agencies the way some other jurisdictions do.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.section: The National Strategy for Data and AI
chunks.text:
SDAIA announced the National Strategy for Data and Artificial Intelligence
(NSDAI) in October 2020 at the first Global AI Summit in Riyadh, under the
banner "Where the best of Data and AI is made reality." The strategy aims to
position Saudi Arabia as a global leader in data and AI by 2030, using a
phased approach: addressing national urgencies first, then building
longer-term competitive foundations. Measurable targets cover investment
raised, the number of trained data and AI specialists, the number of AI
startups, and the Kingdom's standing in open-data and research-publication
rankings.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.text:
SDAIA has built a national data governance framework covering collection,
storage, sharing, quality, privacy, and security standards across both
government and private-sector entities. This framework is designed to make
high-quality data available for AI development while still protecting
individual privacy, and it works alongside Saudi Arabia's Personal Data
Protection Law, which SDAIA helped develop and which draws on international
best practice while accommodating the Kingdom's specific legal context.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.text:
Progress against NSDAI targets is tracked through an AI readiness index for
government entities and dashboards published on the National Data Governance
Platform. SDAIA conducts periodic reviews and publishes public reporting
intended to support international benchmarking, signalling that the strategy
is meant to be evaluated against external as well as internal standards.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.text:
SDAIA has released a draft National AI Risk Management Framework that
introduces a risk-based classification system distinguishing low-risk from
high-risk AI applications, each carrying different compliance expectations
for developers and deployers. As of the most recent guidance, Saudi Arabia
does not yet have a single standalone law covering all AI systems; instead,
AI-relevant obligations are distributed across the PDPL, the NSDAI's
governance framework, and this emerging risk-classification framework, with
observers expecting consolidation toward a dedicated AI law over time.

chunks.doc_title: Saudi Arabia's National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI) and SDAIA
chunks.text:
A 2025 institutional shift split Saudi Arabia's AI development across two
tracks: SDAIA and NCAI retain research authority, while HUMAIN, a
state-backed company launched under the Public Investment Fund, was
positioned as the production and commercial distribution channel for advanced
Saudi AI models, including the Arabic-language model ALLaM. This split
mirrors how some other countries separate state research institutes from
commercial champions, and 2026 was designated the Kingdom's "Year of
Artificial Intelligence" to mark the shift from strategy to execution.

chunks.doc_title: UAE AI Governance Institutions and the National AI Security Policy
chunks.text:
UAE AI governance is spread across several bodies rather than concentrated in
a single regulator. The Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence holds
overall policy responsibility and chairs coordination with the Emirates
Council for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transactions, which aligns
federal and emirate-level implementation. Data protection sits separately
with the UAE Data Office, created under Federal Decree-Law No. 44 of 2021.
Security-specific oversight of AI systems is led by the Cyber Security
Council, which issued the National Artificial Intelligence Security Policy in
2025.

chunks.doc_title: UAE AI Governance Institutions and the National AI Security Policy
chunks.text:
In September 2024, the UAE Cabinet issued an international policy on AI that
builds on the country's earlier AI charter and sets out a strategic framework
for pursuing the UAE's AI targets while following internationally recognised
best practices. As part of this framework, the UAE introduced a "Seal of
Approval" intended to recognise AI companies that meet high standards of
quality and ethics, giving the government a way to reward responsible
development rather than relying solely on penalties for non-compliance.

chunks.doc_title: UAE AI Governance Institutions and the National AI Security Policy
chunks.text:
The Cyber Security Council's 2025 policy complements the National AI Strategy
2031 by focusing specifically on the secure, controlled, and trustworthy
deployment of AI systems. Its core themes are risk management, mandatory
human oversight for consequential decisions, and protection against misuse of
AI capabilities. Where the National AI Strategy sets ambition and the PDPL
governs personal data, this policy is the instrument most directly concerned
with AI system security posture: how models are deployed, monitored, and
constrained against adversarial or unintended use.

chunks.doc_title: UAE AI Governance Institutions and the National AI Security Policy
chunks.text:
Abu Dhabi's sovereign wealth funds, Mubadala and ADQ, play a direct role in
translating policy into infrastructure. Both funds finance large-scale AI
compute and data infrastructure, establish or back AI-focused companies and
research funds, and form partnerships with established international AI
players. This sovereign-capital backing is one of the more distinctive
features of the UAE's approach compared with jurisdictions where AI policy is
purely regulatory: the government is simultaneously the rule-setter and one
of the largest capital allocators in the domestic AI ecosystem, including
through the US-UAE AI Acceleration Partnership aimed at building AI
infrastructure with US public and private partners.

chunks.doc_title: UAE AI Governance Institutions and the National AI Security Policy
chunks.text:
A useful way to separate these instruments: the National AI Strategy 2031 sets
the destination and economic targets; the PDPL governs how personal data may
be used, including in AI training and inference; the National AI Security
Policy governs how AI systems themselves must be secured and overseen once
deployed; and the Seal of Approval and sovereign fund activity are the
incentive and capital mechanisms meant to pull the ecosystem toward that
destination faster than regulation alone would achieve.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
Announced by the UAE Cabinet in October 2017 and formally adopted in 2019, this
strategy is the country's overarching framework for becoming a global hub for
artificial intelligence by 2031. It sits inside the broader UAE Centennial 2071
vision and is overseen by the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, a
role the UAE created as the first of its kind in the world. Implementation is
coordinated through the Emirates Council for Artificial Intelligence and Digital
Transactions, which keeps federal and emirate-level bodies moving in step with
one another.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
The strategy lays out eight objectives: build a reputation as an AI destination,
strengthen the UAE's competitive position in priority sectors through AI
deployment, grow a fertile domestic AI ecosystem, embed AI across government
services to improve citizens' daily lives, attract and train AI talent, bring
world-leading research capability into target industries, supply the data and
infrastructure needed to make the UAE a testbed for AI, and put in place strong
governance and effective regulation.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
Workforce development is treated as central to the whole effort. Plans include
public AI literacy campaigns, specialised upskilling for STEM graduates and
government staff, and partnerships with international experts. Two flagship
mechanisms support this: a National Virtual AI Institute meant to pool global
and local research expertise, and a Key Thinkers Program that brings leading
researchers into direct collaboration with UAE institutions. An open-access AI
library is also planned to make accumulated knowledge broadly available rather
than siloed inside individual agencies.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
AI adoption is targeted at concrete societal problems such as healthcare
improvement and traffic safety, partly through national AI challenges that
invite solutions to specific problems. On the economic side, the strategy aims
to lift AI's contribution to GDP from roughly 9 percent toward 45 percent by
2031, a shift estimated to add about AED 335 billion in economic value. Related
targets include training 10,000 UAE-based data scientists and machine learning
engineers, supported by golden visa pathways for international experts, and
moving public services toward a fully paper-free standard across all emirates.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
The strategy commits to annual AI Value Reports that track outcomes such as
jobs created, patents filed, and carbon savings, intended to keep the roadmap
accountable rather than aspirational. It also anticipates that AI agents will
increasingly carry out operational government functions directly, such as
screening visa applications or pre-clearing shipping manifests, which raises
the stakes for the governance and oversight mechanisms described elsewhere in
UAE policy, particularly the National AI Security Policy and the Personal Data
Protection Law.

chunks.doc_title: UAE National Strategy for Artificial Intelligence 2031
chunks.text:
This strategy is the umbrella document; it does not itself set out data
protection rules or AI-specific security requirements. Those are handled by
separate instruments, namely Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 (the Personal
Data Protection Law) and the National Artificial Intelligence Security Policy
issued by the Cyber Security Council. Readers looking for compliance detail
should consult those documents rather than this strategic overview.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
The UAE Cabinet enacted Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 in November 2021,
giving the country its first comprehensive federal data protection law. It
took effect on 2 January 2022 following a six-month grace period for
organisations to reach compliance. The law is commonly referred to as the
PDPL. A companion law, Federal Decree-Law No. 44 of 2021, established the UAE
Data Office as the dedicated regulator responsible for proposing data
protection policy, approving compliance standards, handling complaints, and
issuing implementation guidance.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
The PDPL applies to any data controller or processor located in the UAE that
processes personal data, regardless of whether the individuals concerned are
inside or outside the country. It also reaches organisations established
outside the UAE if they process personal data belonging to UAE residents,
giving it an extraterritorial reach similar in spirit to the EU's GDPR. Several
categories sit outside its scope: government data, public-sector entities,
purely personal use of data, health and credit data (which are governed by
their own sector-specific laws), and entities operating in free zones that
already maintain their own data protection regimes, such as the Dubai
International Financial Centre.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
Organisations subject to the PDPL must establish a valid legal basis before
processing personal data, put in place appropriate technical and
organisational safeguards, appoint a Data Protection Officer where the volume
or sensitivity of processing warrants it, and carry out Data Protection Impact
Assessments for higher-risk processing activities. The law also sets
conditions, rather than an outright ban, on transferring personal data outside
the UAE, with transfers permitted to jurisdictions the UAE Data Office
recognises as offering adequate protection.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
Data subjects gain a defined set of rights under the law, including the right
to be informed about how their data is processed and a right relevant
specifically to automated decision-making: individuals may object to being
subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including
AI-driven decisions, where that decision produces legal or similarly
significant effects. This provision is one of the clearest points of contact
between the PDPL and AI governance more broadly, since it constrains how
automated systems can be deployed against UAE residents without human
oversight.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
The UAE Data Office has moved relatively quickly on enforcement and guidance
compared with the slower early years some other jurisdictions experienced
after passing similar laws. Administrative fines apply for violations, with
exact amounts left to executive regulations; violations can also expose
organisations to civil liability and regulatory inspections. Practitioners
note that GDPR compliance does not automatically satisfy PDPL requirements,
particularly around cross-border transfer rules, since adequacy is determined
by the UAE Data Office rather than by reference to EU adequacy findings.

chunks.doc_title: UAE Personal Data Protection Law (Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021)
chunks.text:
For organisations deploying AI systems in the UAE, the PDPL's most consequential
provisions concern consent for data used in training or inference, data
residency requirements that can affect where models and pipelines may run,
and the right to an explanation when automated decisions carry significant
consequences. The PDPL itself is not an AI-specific law; AI-focused security
expectations are instead set out separately in the National Artificial
Intelligence Security Policy of 2025.
